attributes.statement: Possessive suffixes consist of possessive suffix proper + definite article suffix. The definite article shows case difference.
When possessive suffix is added to a noun denoting a relative or body part, the possessive suffix on its own is used without the definite article part.
The -ii type definite article endings may be used in possessive suffixes where appropriate for referential definiteness.
Possessive suffixes are used with nouns of position and time to form phrases translating as prepositions (e.g., gudahayda 'inside me/it').
Each prepositional phrase has masculine and feminine forms according to the noun going with the phrase.
Both types of genitive constructions are equally used in Somali: noun+possessive suffix and noun+noun.
Negative present progressive: change positive present tense endings to negative present tense endings (familiar from general present) and use with ma.
Alternative negative present progressive: auxiliary form (maayo/maysid/mayso etc.) immediately follows the infinitive.
Negative past progressive: use ma with unchanging form verb+ayn or verb+aynin (conjugation 1: stem+ayn/in; conjugations 2-3: infinitive+ayn/in).
There are five prefixing verbs where person marker is added as a prefix: yiil, yimi, yidhi, yiqiin, yahay.
jir stresses that a thing exists; yiil stresses that an object is in a particular place; joog is used for animate subjects in a place.
When plural endings are added to yimi, the final -i of the stem is deleted (yimaaddeen/timaaddeen).
The infinitive of yimi is iman, used with auxiliary verbs and as base for progressive aspect.
yidhi is used only with direct speech. Indirect speech uses sheeg with an in-clause.
To translate 'to' as in 'I said to him', the preverbal preposition ku is used.
Basic word order of waxa-focus construction: WAXA (+verbal pronoun) VERB FOCUSED NOUN PHRASE.
When subject is focused with waxa: subject is in absolutive form, verb uses reduced paradigm, waxa lacks subject verbal pronoun.
Subordinate clauses are all essentially noun phrases and can play the same roles as noun phrases in a sentence.
Mood classifiers and focus markers are not used in subordinate clauses; negative word is aan instead of ma.
All subordinate clauses are essentially relative clauses.
In in-clauses, case marking goes on the final verb since it is the last part of the subordinate clause noun phrase.
Word order in in-clauses: SUBJECT OBJECT VERB (object may also come after verb).
General present and present progressive subordinate forms are the same as main clause negative forms: -aa changes to -o, -aan to -aan.
General past and past progressive subordinate forms differ from main clause only in stress-tone pattern.
'In order to' is rendered by an in-clause with preverbal preposition u.
'Have to, must' is rendered by in-clause with classifier waa (waa in...).
Fixed order in preposition/pronoun clusters: PRONOUN + PREPOSITIONS (in order: u, ku, ka, la).
Whenever a preverbal preposition is in a cluster with pronouns or other preverbal prepositions, there is only one stress-tone on the final vowel.
Restrictive relative clauses use oo; appositive (non-restrictive) relative clauses use ee.
oo is not a relative pronoun; there is no relative pronoun in Somali. oo only distinguishes clause types.
Appositive relative clauses cannot be used with undefined head nouns.
Restrictive relative clauses may not be used with names.
In relative clauses when subject is a pronoun, subject verbal pronouns are used on their own (no classifier or focus marker).
When head noun is not subject of RC and RC is not subject of sentence: present = main clause negative forms; past = stress-tone on final vowel, reduced paradigm absolutive.
When head noun is not subject of RC but RC is subject of sentence: verb form same as main clause in all respects (subject marking on verb).
When head noun is subject of RC and RC is not subject of main sentence: reduced paradigm (absolutive) is used.
When head noun is subject of RC and RC is subject of main sentence: reduced paradigm (subject) with main clause endings.
When a subject relative clause is focused, the verb is not marked as subject because the RC is focused.
When yaa is subject of sentence, reduced paradigm is used (incorporates focus marker baa).
When answering questions, the information asked for must be focused.
Independent pronouns may be used for emphasis and for focusing a pronoun.
Independent pronouns are basically nouns with the definite article suffix attached (all masculine except iyada).
'While' construction: independent pronoun + appositive relative clause with oo joined to pronoun.
General past of yahay has no person marker prefix; person marker appears as suffix (aha, ahayd, ahayn, etc.).
General present of yahay uses person marker prefixes; stem changes from ah to i in 2nd/3rd plural.
Reduced paradigm of yahay present: invariable ah (absolutive) and ihi (subject).
There is no progressive form of yahay because it is a stative verb.
Subordinate clause forms of yahay are the same as main clause forms except reduced paradigm past tense (subject form without stress-tone).
Predicative adjectives use yahay as a copula; predicative adjectives can be written separately from or joined to yahay.
Short forms of yahay with adjectives: delete ah from the full form (e.g., dheer yahay -> dheeryay).
Attributive adjectives with yahay in relative clauses: zero/nothing is the absolutive form (adjective alone), -i is the subject form.
Comparative is formed with preverbal preposition ka + adjective.
Superlative is formed with preverbal preposition cluster ugu + adjective.
'Very' is expressed with aad + ii + adjective; aad is focused with baa or ayaa.
For further emphasis, use aad iyo aad ('very very').
Stress-tone pattern of adjectives is almost always stress-tone on the final vowel.
'Which' is expressed with suffix -kee (m.) / -tee (f.). When used on its own means 'which one(s)?'.
'Where' uses xaggee or halkee with -kee suffix, or mee on its own.

attributes.statement: Shortened forms of yahay in general present are formed by deleting the ah part in the middle. Pattern: person marker + ay = ending (e.g., -tay, -yay, -nay, -tiin, -yiin).
In the negative, shortened versions are optional and formed by deleting ah from the full negative general present form.
When yahay is used with adjectives in subordinate clauses, the contracted form of the verb is ALWAYS used, in both present and past tense.
The comparative is formed using the preverbal preposition ka with the adjective. The adjective retains its yahay agreement.
The superlative is expressed using the preverbal preposition cluster ugu with the adjective. Ugu may be used on its own with adjectives.
To express 'very', use aad with preverbal preposition i. The word aad must always be focused using baa or ayaa.
The suffix -kee/-tee is used for 'which'. -kee is added to masculine nouns and -tee to feminine nouns. Usually focused.
'Where' is expressed with xaggee (from xag 'place') or halkee (from hal 'place'). Answer must focus the location.
Mass nouns are used with a form of yahay (typically ah) in a relative clause construction. When a number precedes the unit of measure, oo is used.
Collective nouns behave the same way as mass nouns and take the same yahay relative clause construction.
Adverbial conjunctions (when, if, after, etc.) are translated by relative clauses with specific head nouns functioning like conjunctions. Subject verbal pronoun added to the head noun.
When is rendered by marka with relative clause; subject verbal pronoun added to marka. Markii (with -kii definite) may also be used, with pronoun written separately.
The negative word in subordinate clauses is aan (not ma). Aan immediately follows the head noun and is attached if the noun ends in a short vowel. In appositive relative clauses, aan follows oo.
Shortened subject verbal pronouns used with aan: -aynu (I/we incl.), -aad (you sg.), -aannu (we excl.), -aydin (you pl.), -ay (he/she/they). First three differ from main clause forms.
The negative form using maayoo cannot be used in relative clauses for present progressive. Use keenayo, keenayse, etc., or the invariable past progressive form keenayn/keenaynin.
For focusing in yes-no questions with baa: Ma NP baa ...? When subject is focused, all characteristics from statements also apply in questions.
For focusing in yes-no questions with miyaa: NP miyaa/d + subject verbal pronoun ...? If subject is focused, familiar characteristics (reduced paradigm) are present.
Negative questions without noun phrase focus use sew...ma: Sew maad tegin? (Didn't you go?) Sew may be separated from ma by intervening noun phrases.
If a noun phrase is focused in a negative question, aan is added to the focus marker. Shortened subject verbal pronouns are used with negative + focus combinations.
Optative: pronoun (inherent part except 3rd person) + verb stem + ending. Endings: -o (1SG/3SG.M), -to (2SG/3SG.F), -no (1PL), -teen (2PL), -een (3PL). 3rd person uses ha + verb.
Optative stress-tone is on the vowel immediately before the ending, except 3rd person where stress-tone is on ha instead.
Negative optative uses invariable verb form (same as negative general past, stress-tone on final vowel of stem for conjugation 1). Preceded by negative words incorporating subject pronouns.
Potential: verb stem + ee/ee endings with vowel harmony. Endings: -ee (1SG/3SG.M), -tee (2SG/3SG.F), -nee (1PL), -teen (2PL), -een (3PL). Classifier shuw always present.

Conditional 'would have': infinitive + leh with contracted yahay forms. No tense distinction. Forms: lahaa (1SG/3SG.M), lahayd (2SG/3SG.F), lahayn (1PL.INCL), lahaydeen (2PL), lahaayeen (3PL/1PL.EXCL).
Negative conditional uses ma + infinitive + -een/teén endings. Pattern parallels conditional affirmative but with negative marker ma.
Reduced paradigm is used when the head noun is the subject of the relative clause. All verbs follow the same reduced pattern regardless of conjugation.
Full paradigm (absolutive) used when head noun is NOT the subject of the relative clause and head noun + clause is NOT the subject of the main clause.
Full paradigm (subject) used when head noun is NOT the subject of the relative clause but head noun + clause IS the subject of the main clause. Same as main clause full paradigm.
The pronoun la ('one') behaves like na in clusters but must come before any object pronoun.
Possessive suffixes have short versions without the definite article. Masculine: kay/kaa/kiis/keed/keen/kayo/kin/kood. Feminine: tay/taa/tiis/teed/teen/tayo/tiin/tiod.
Note the geminate bb in the verb cab: the b is geminated when an ending beginning with a vowel follows.

attributes.name: Somali Alphabet Size
attributes.description: The Somali alphabet contains 26 letters plus the glottal stop (hamza). Native Somali words never use p, v, z.

attributes.name: Vowel Length Contrast
attributes.description: Somali has five short vowels (a, e, i, o, u) and five long vowels (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu). Vowel length is phonemically significant.

attributes.name: Consonant Doubling Contrast
attributes.description: Somali distinguishes short and long (doubled) consonants: e.g., abaar (drought) vs abbaar (aim at).

attributes.name: Glottal Stop Position
attributes.description: The glottal stop (hamza) can never be word-initial in Somali.

attributes.name: Tone and Grammatical Gender
attributes.description: In Somali, tone is used to distinguish grammatical gender. Words spelled the same in root form are distinguished by different gender endings and/or tone.

attributes.name: Focus Marker Position
attributes.description: baa marks FOCUS (new or emphasized information) and comes AFTER the head noun.

attributes.name: Declarative Marker Position
attributes.description: waa marks positive declarative statements and comes BEFORE the head noun/predicate.

attributes.name: Question Marker Function
attributes.description: ma marks positive (non-negative) yes/no questions.

attributes.name: Grammatical Gender is Arbitrary
attributes.description: Somali is a language based on grammatical gender. The way a noun is handled does not always make semantic sense. Gender has far-reaching grammatical impact on plural forms and verb agreement.

attributes.name: Masculine Article -ka
attributes.description: Masculine nouns take article suffixes beginning with -k. The standard form -ka marks NEW INFORMATION. The form -kii marks GIVEN/PREVIOUSLY KNOWN information.

attributes.name: Feminine Article -ta
attributes.description: Feminine nouns take article suffixes beginning with -t. The standard form -ta marks NEW INFORMATION. The form -tii marks GIVEN/PREVIOUSLY KNOWN information.

attributes.name: Four Forms per Noun
attributes.description: Each Somali noun ultimately requires learning four forms: (1) singular root, (2) with article, (3) plural form, (4) plural with article.

attributes.name: Masculine Noun: -e to -a
attributes.description: With masculine nouns ending in -e, the final vowel changes to -a and the article changes to -ha: fure → furaha.

attributes.name: Masculine Noun: -e to -i (known)
attributes.description: With masculine nouns ending in -e, for known information, the final vowel changes to -i and the article changes to -hii: fure → furihii.

attributes.name: Masculine Noun: -o to -a
attributes.description: With masculine nouns ending in -o, the final vowel changes to -a and the article changes to -ha: biyo → biyaha.

attributes.name: Masculine Noun: -o to -i (known)
attributes.description: With masculine nouns ending in -o, for known information, the final vowel changes to -i and the article changes to -hii: biyo → biyihii.

attributes.name: k→g Assimilation
attributes.description: If a masculine noun ends in -g, -w, -y, or -i, the k of the article changes to g: buug → buugga, guri → guriga.

attributes.name: k Drops After Certain Consonants
attributes.description: If a masculine noun ends in -c, -h, -q, -kh, or -x, the k of the article is lost, leaving only the vowel: magac → magaca, shaah → shaaha, suuq → suuqa, madax → madaxa.

attributes.name: Vowel Harmony in Masculine Nouns
attributes.description: The final vowel of the root changes to match the vowel of the suffix (e→a with -ha, e→i with -hii, o→a with -ha, o→i with -hii).

attributes.name: Feminine Noun: -o to -a
attributes.description: With feminine nouns ending in -o, the final vowel changes to -a and the article changes to -da: cunto → cuntada.

attributes.name: Feminine t→d Change
attributes.description: If a feminine noun ends in a vowel (other than -o) or with -d, -h, -kh, -x, -w, -y, or glottal stop, the t changes to d: mindi → mindida, subax → subaxda.

attributes.name: Feminine t→dha Change
attributes.description: In dialects with feminine nouns ending in -dh, the -ta suffix changes to -dha: gabadh → gabadhdha. In other dialects these words end in -r.

attributes.name: l + t → sh Assimilation
attributes.description: When a feminine noun ends in -l, the combination of final -l plus suffix -t changes both sounds to -sh-: basal + ta → basasha, il + ta → isha, meel + ta → meesha.

attributes.name: Vowel Harmony in Feminine Nouns
attributes.description: The final vowel -o of the root changes to -a to match the suffix vowel -a: cunto → cuntada, daawo → daawada.

attributes.name: Singular Imperative as Citation Form
attributes.description: The singular imperative is the main citation form for each verb; needed to find a verb in a Somali dictionary and upon which most other tenses are built.

attributes.name: Plural Imperative with -a
attributes.description: The plural imperative is generally formed by adding -a to the singular imperative (for consonant-final verbs): gal → gala, bax → baxa.

attributes.name: Plural Imperative with -ya
attributes.description: If a verb ends in -i or -e, add -ya to form the plural imperative: akhri → akhriya, sii → siiya, bislee → bisleeya.

attributes.name: Past Tense Verb Endings
attributes.description: For the past tense there are five endings: -ay/-ey (1SG/3SG.M), -tay/-tey (2SG/3SG.F), -nay/-ney (1PL), -teen (2PL), -een (3PL/2PL variant). These are built from compounding: -t- signals 2nd person and 3rd feminine, -n signals 1st person plural, -ay/-ey signals past tense except for -een.

attributes.name: Seven Verbal Pronouns
attributes.description: There are seven verbal pronouns that fuse with classifiers: aan (I), aad (you SG), uu (he), ay (she/they), aannu (we excl), aynu (we incl), aydin (you PL). When added to waa, only w- is left.

attributes.name: Pronoun Fusion with waa
attributes.description: When verbal pronouns are added to the declarative classifier waa, only w- remains: waan (waa+aan), waad (waa+aad), wuu (waa+uu), wey (waa+ay), waannu (waa+aannu), weynu (waa+aynu), weydin (waa+aydin).

attributes.name: Pronoun Fusion with baa
attributes.description: When verbal pronouns are added to the focus classifier baa, only b- remains: baan (baa+aan), baad (baa+aad), buu (baa+uu), bey (baa+ay), baannu (baa+aannu), beynu (baa+aynu), beydin (baa+aydin).

attributes.name: Pronoun Fusion with ma
attributes.description: When verbal pronouns are added to the interrogative ma, only m- remains: maan (ma+aan), maad (ma+aad), muu (ma+uu), mey (ma+ay), maannu (ma+aannu), meynu (ma+aynu), meydin (ma+aydin).

attributes.name: Subject Marker -u
attributes.description: The suffix -u marks the SUBJECT case on nouns and pronouns: magacaygu (my name), adigu (you-SUBJ).

attributes.name: Definite: New vs Given Information
attributes.description: Somali distinguishes two kinds of definite information: new (just being introduced, marked by -a/-ka/-ta) and given (known or already discussed, marked by -ii/-kii/-tii).

attributes.name: Natural vs Grammatical Gender
attributes.description: Names follow natural gender (man's name = masculine, woman's name = feminine). Many nouns follow meaningful patterns. However, Somali is based on grammatical gender where assignment is arbitrary: e.g., beri (day) is masculine, maalin (day) is feminine.

attributes.name: Verb Categories
attributes.description: Each Somali verb has the following characteristics: Person (1st, 2nd, 3rd), Gender (masculine vs feminine, only on 3rd singular), Number (singular vs plural), Tense (past, present, habitual), and Conjugation (based on imperative singular ending: consonant-final = Conj 1, vowel-final = Conj 2-3, irregular = Conj 4-5).

attributes.name: baan is baa + aan
attributes.description: baan is the result of FUSION of baa (the Focus marker) and the PRONOUN aan (I).

attributes.name: Homonyms Distinguished by Gender
attributes.description: Sometimes gender is used to keep words that would otherwise be identical distinct: hal (/sha) = female camel vs hal (ka) = one; waa = declarative marker vs waa (ga) = time, era.

attributes.name: Feminine Occupation Suffix -ad
attributes.description: Feminine occupation forms have the suffix -ad: askariyad (female soldier), dhabbaakhad (female cook), dhakhtarad (female doctor), karraaniyad (female clerk), macallimad (female teacher).

attributes.statement: Factitive suffix -ee transforms nouns or adjectives into verbs with general sense of to make become X. There is no consistent change in meaning, although there is a general sense of to be X, to become X, or to make something become X.
Autobenefactive suffix -so generally denotes to do X to or for oneself. In some cases the English translation does not always contain for oneself.
Adjectival (passive) verbs follow the pattern: TRANSITIVE VERB > DERIVED ADJECTIVE + -an > ADJECTIVAL VERB with -may suffix, meaning get Xed or become X.
The conjunction oo is used to link equal sentence parts, appositive constructions, and indefinite restrictive constructions.
In several dialects ee can be substituted for oo with no difference in meaning or function.
Relative clauses take the reduced verb endings associated with SUBJECT/FOCUS verbs.
Prepositions fuse with pronouns and with each other to form combined portmanteau forms. Two-place and three-place combinations exist.

The negative conditional would not have uses prefix ma-/me- with person-specific endings: maanan (1sg), maadan (2sg), muusan (3sg.m), meeyan (3sg.f), maannan (1pl.excl), meynan (1pl.incl), meydnan (2pl), meeyan (3pl), followed by the verb root with -een suffix.

The -na suffix with negative meaning all by itself. If a verb is added, another negative marker will also be used. It attaches to nouns to create universal negative meaning: ninna (no one), meelna (nowhere), marna (never), waxna (nothing).
Oon is the fusion of oo and aan, used to mean without or although not. It creates subordinate clauses of concession or condition.
The negative imperative uses the prefix ha- before the verb stem with -in suffix for singular and -ina for plural.
The negative ma with the verb to be (ahayn) is used for predicative negation: NP + maaha (is not).
Negative focus pronoun forms combine focus marker (baa) + negative pronoun: Cali keliya baanan arkin (only Ali I did not see).
Many verb roots from Conjugation One can be used alone as masculine nouns (mostly Declension 2) with similar meaning or sense of act of Xing.
The suffix -id forms feminine nouns (Declension 1) from Conjugation One stems with the general meaning act of Xing or -ion. Sound changes affect some derivations.
The suffix -is forms feminine nouns (Declension 1) from Conjugation One stems with the meaning act of Xing, as an alternate to -id.
The suffix -in forms feminine nouns from Conjugation Two-A stems with the meaning act of Xing.
The suffix -asho forms generic feminine nouns from verb stems (especially Conjugation 3) with the meaning VERB-ing.
The suffix -nimo added to noun stems denotes a quality or state equivalent to English -ity, -ness, -hood or -ship. It creates feminine nouns of Declension 6.
The suffix -e added to verb roots forms masculine nouns of Declension 7 with the meaning doer of X, similar to English -er or -or.
The suffix -tan generally denotes reciprocal or mutual activity. It is very limited in use.
The suffix -tooyo is found on a limited number of nouns showing a state of being X, akin to -hood or -ship.
Noun plus verb compounds yield nouns indicating professions or habitual activities: af+yaqaan = linguist.
Noun plus adjective compounds yield nouns: bad+weyn = ocean, bad+yar = lake.
Noun + adjective compounds yield adjectives: fool+xun = ugly, hadal+badan = talkative.
Nouns of Declension 3 and verbs of Conjugation 3-B regularly lose the final vowel of the stem; this also happens in derivation of adjectives and other parts of speech.
Short vowels often change to match the vowels of a suffix or the following word.
In derivation of feminine nouns and verbs with feminine or second person endings, a stem final -l and suffix initial -t change to sh.
The addition of a suffix beginning with n to roots ending in -l results in ll and to those ending in -r results in rr.
Following consonants g, w, y and vowel i, in derivation of masculine nouns, the k changes to g.
Following all vowels (except i), in derivations of masculine nouns, the k changes to h.
The change of a to e occurs in derivation of Conjugation 2-A transitive verbs, infinitives or past negatives of Conjugation 1, and derived nouns with -is or -id.
In deriving verbs of Conjugation 2-A, the addition of -i to make a transitive or causative verb triggers a change of final -g to -j. This same process triggers a change of final -q to -j.
Two -t- sounds coming together result in consonant loss, affecting verb inflections. This mainly affects autobenefactive verb forms.
In a few derivations, after vowel loss occurs, the two middle consonants switch places.
Full pronouns have shorter versions which subtract the determiner suffix and in some cases the final vowel. These forms can only be used with conjunction suffixes like -na and -se in most dialects.
Only first and second person singular pronouns can be contracted in focus constructions: Anaa tegey = aniga + baa.
In inflection of feminine nouns and verbs of Conjugation 3 with a stem ending in -o, that vowel changes to -a- when suffixes are added.
With noun stems ending in -e, the final vowel changes to -a to match the vowel(s) in the suffix. This is a type of vowel harmony.

labels.default: Definite article agrees with noun gender
labels.english: Definite article agrees with noun gender

attributes.description: Masculine nouns take -ka/-kii definite articles; feminine nouns take -ta/-tii. This is grammatical gender, not semantic.

labels.default: Focus classifiers immediately follow the focused element
labels.english: Focus classifiers immediately follow the focused element

attributes.description: Focus markers (waa, baa, ayaa, waxa) immediately follow the element being focused. baa focuses on subject or non-subject; ayaa emphasizes immediately preceding word; waxa is used for cleft/focus constructions.

labels.default: Declarative sentences use waa as focus marker
labels.english: Declarative sentences use waa as focus marker

attributes.description: Simple declarative statements are marked with waa. In negative declaratives, waa is replaced by ma + aan negative forms.

labels.default: Negation uses ma + aan + verb stem
labels.english: Negation uses ma + aan + verb stem

attributes.description: Negative sentences use ma as the negative particle combined with aan forms (aan, aanan, aannu, etc.) fused with verbal pronouns.

labels.default: Questions are formed with ma particle
labels.english: Questions are formed with ma particle

attributes.description: Yes/no questions are formed with the interrogative particle ma. Content questions use interrogative words (maxay, goorma, xaggee, immisa, yaa, sidee, kee).

labels.default: Verbs agree with subject in person, number, and gender
labels.english: Verbs agree with subject in person, number, and gender

attributes.description: Verbs in Somali agree with their subjects in person (1st, 2nd, 3rd), number (singular, plural), and gender (masculine, feminine for 3rd singular).

labels.default: Possessive pronouns are suffixed to the noun
labels.english: Possessive pronouns are suffixed to the noun

attributes.description: Possessive pronouns are expressed as suffixes on the noun: -ayga/-aygu/-aygii (my M), -aad/-aada (your), -iis (his), -eed (her), -eenn (our exc), -een (our inc), -ood (their/your pl).

labels.default: Genitive constructions place the possessor after the possessed noun
labels.english: Genitive constructions place the possessor after the possessed noun

attributes.description: In genitive constructions, the possessed noun precedes the possessor. The definite article on the first noun carries genitive marking (-a instead of -u/-i for subject marking).

labels.default: Habitual present expresses repeated or general action
labels.english: Habitual present expresses repeated or general action

attributes.description: The habitual present is used for repeated actions, general truths, and habitual behavior. It is not explicitly marked for tense but uses the basic verb stem with subject clitics.

labels.default: Future tense is marked with doon
labels.english: Future tense is marked with doon

attributes.description: The future tense uses doon as an auxiliary following the verb stem. Negative future uses doon + ma + aan negative forms.

labels.default: Imperative uses bare verb stem without subject marking
labels.english: Imperative uses bare verb stem without subject marking

attributes.description: The imperative mood uses the bare verb stem without subject clitics. Negative imperative uses haa- + -n + verb stem. Directional particles soo and sii often accompany imperatives.

labels.default: Optative is formed with haa- prefix
labels.english: Optative is formed with haa- prefix

attributes.description: The optative mood expressing wishes or exhortations uses the prefix haa- with the verb stem. Forms include: ha (you sg), ha...een (you pl), ha...o (he/she), ha...nno (we), ha...na (they).

labels.default: Relative clauses use verbal pronoun suffixes
labels.english: Relative clauses use verbal pronoun suffixes

attributes.description: Relative clauses in Somali are marked by special reduced verbal pronoun forms suffixed to the verb, rather than by relative pronouns.

labels.default: Passive equivalent uses la impersonal subject
labels.english: Passive equivalent uses la impersonal subject

attributes.description: Somali does not have a true passive voice. Instead, it uses la 'someone, people' as an impersonal subject with active verb morphology.

labels.default: D/T sound changes occur in conjugation
labels.english: D/T sound changes occur in conjugation

attributes.description: Sound changes involving d and t occur in verb conjugation, especially in conjugation 3 verbs with T+ change and loss of d next to t.
Numbers from 1-9 agree in gender with the noun they modify. The feminine form of 'one' is used with masculine nouns and vice versa.

labels.default: Noun plurals follow eight declension patterns
labels.english: Noun plurals follow eight declension patterns

attributes.description: Somali noun plurals follow eight declension patterns: 1 (-o), 2 (-ayaal/-ooyin), 3 (-ayaal), 4 (-aC#), 5 (-oyin), 6 (-o), 7 (-yaal), 8 (irregular). Each noun belongs to a specific declension class.

labels.default: Verbal nouns are formed with suffixes from verb stems
labels.english: Verbal nouns are formed with suffixes from verb stems

attributes.description: Verbal nouns are formed with suffixes -id, -is (conj 1), -ad, -asho (conj 3), -aal, -itaan from verb stems. Agentive nouns use -e, privative nouns use -darro.

labels.default: Final consonant may reduplicate before certain suffixes
labels.english: Final consonant may reduplicate before certain suffixes

attributes.description: Final consonants of verb stems may reduplicate (double) before certain suffixes and in certain morphological contexts.
Ownership or possession is expressed with the adjective leh 'having'. Negative is ma leh or lahow in conditional contexts.
Temporal clauses expressing 'when' are introduced by marka. The verb in the temporal clause uses reduced (relative) pronoun forms.

labels.default: Tag questions use sow ma aha
labels.english: Tag questions use sow ma aha

attributes.description: Tag questions seeking confirmation are formed with sow ma aha 'isn't it?'. The particle sow introduces a suppositive/rhetorical question.
The superlative degree is formed with u 'for' before the adjective, giving the sense of 'most X'. ugu combines u + ka for 'the most'.
The negative marker aan fuses with verbal pronouns and other grammatical forms, creating contracted negative forms.

labels.default: Some dialects merge h and dh sounds
labels.english: Some dialects merge h and dh sounds

attributes.description: Certain Somali dialects merge or interchange the h and dh sounds, leading to variation in pronunciation.
Existential statements ('there is/are') use wax as a dummy subject with jir 'to exist' or a similar predicate.
Somali is generally predicate-final, with the main verb or predicate coming at the end of the clause or sentence.

labels.default: Focus and non-focus forms may coexist in discourse
labels.english: Focus and non-focus forms may coexist in discourse

attributes.description: Both focus constructions (with baa/ayaa/waxa) and non-focus declaratives (with waa) may appear in the same discourse, with focus used for emphasis or new information.
Rhetorical questions are marked by the particle show (variant of sow) combined with the -ee suffix on the verb.
Conditional clauses expressing 'if' are introduced by haddii, which fuses with verbal pronouns. The verb uses reduced forms.

labels.default: Head nouns precede modifiers in noun phrases
labels.english: Head nouns precede modifiers in noun phrases

attributes.description: In Somali noun phrases, the head noun precedes its modifiers (adjectives, relative clauses, possessives).

labels.default: Short forms of 'to be' are used as suffixes
labels.english: Short forms of 'to be' are used as suffixes

attributes.description: The verb 'to be' has short suffixal forms (-ahay, -aad, -ahay, etc.) that attach to nouns and adjectives to form predicates.
Somali verbs are classified into conjugation classes based on stem morphology. Conjugation 1: regular stems. 2a: C+y stems. 2b: C+e stems. 3a/3b: various irregular patterns with T+ changes.
Restrictive relative-like constructions are linked by oo 'while, and' rather than full relative clause morphology.

labels.default: Privative nouns are formed with -darro suffix
labels.english: Privative nouns are formed with -darro suffix

attributes.description: Privative nouns expressing lack or absence are formed with the suffix -darro (declension 6), e.g., af-darro 'lack of speech'.

labels.default: Factitive verbs are formed with -ee suffix
labels.english: Factitive verbs are formed with -ee suffix

attributes.description: Factitive verbs meaning 'cause to be X' or 'become X' are formed with the suffix -ee added to adjective or noun stems.
Autobenefactive verbs expressing action done for oneself use the suffix -at (becomes -o in some contexts).
Indirect or softened commands are expressed using optative mood forms rather than direct imperatives.

labels.default: Appositives follow the noun they modify
labels.english: Appositives follow the noun they modify

attributes.description: Appositive noun phrases providing additional information follow the noun they modify, without special marking.
Emphatic forms of independent pronouns are created by adding -na 'and, also': aniga+na=anigana 'and me', iyada+na=iyadana 'and her'.

labels.default: First person plural distinguishes inclusive and exclusive
labels.english: First person plural distinguishes inclusive and exclusive

attributes.description: First person plural pronouns distinguish inclusive (including addressee: annagu 'we all') and exclusive (excluding addressee: ayaannu 'we but not you').

labels.default: Articles, demonstratives, and verbs agree with noun gender
labels.english: Articles, demonstratives, and verbs agree with noun gender

attributes.description: Grammatical agreement operates between nouns and their articles (-ka/-ta), demonstratives (kani/tani), and verbal pronouns (uu/ay).

labels.default: Different words are used for 'one' with masculine vs feminine nouns
labels.english: Different words are used for 'one' with masculine vs feminine nouns

attributes.description: The numeral 'one' has different forms depending on the gender of the noun it modifies: mid/kow/t.

labels.default: Numbers can be joined to nouns with oo
labels.english: Numbers can be joined to nouns with oo

attributes.description: Numbers above 9 can be joined to nouns with the conjunction oo 'and', forming a compound-like construction.
Verbal nouns derived from conjugation 1 verbs use the suffixes -id and -is (both masculine gender). Conjugation 3 verbal nouns use -ad/-asho (feminine).
Vocative forms of nouns use the suffix -ow (masculine) or -eeyo (feminine) to address someone directly.

chunks.payload: Pages 36-70 of Colloquial Somali cover: plural adjective formation (reduplication), genitive case constructions with suffixes -eéd/-od/-aad, numbers with nouns and their genitive rules, variants of 'one' (kow/hal/mid), verbs that lose vowels before vowel endings (maqal/maql-), irregular plurals from Arabic, general present tense paradigms for conjugations 1/2A/2B, preverbal prepositions (u/ku/ka/la), verbal object pronouns, present progressive tense formation, ordinal numbers with -aad, question word max- with subject pronouns, focus markers baa/ayaa (interchangeable), subject focus with reduced verb paradigm and absolutive case, contractions of baa (ninkaa), conjugation 3B verb formation, numbers above 10 and time expressions, infinitive formation with sound changes, future tense with doon auxiliary, habitual past with jir auxiliary, negative imperative with ha, negative general past with ma, negative general present, past progressive tense, demonstrative suffixes (-kan/-kaas/-keer/-koo), auxiliary verbs rab/kar/waa, impersonal pronoun la for passive constructions, and the Somali naming system.

Possessive suffixes have full forms with definite article and short forms without. Full forms: kayga/tayda (my), kaaga/taada (your), kiisa/tiisa (his), keeda/teeda (her), keenna/teenna (our incl.), kayaga/tayada (our excl.), kiinna/tiinna (your pl.), kooda/tooda (their). Short forms used with body parts and relatives: hooyaday, aabbahay, fartay.

Prepositional phrases formed with possessive suffixes: gudahayda/debeddeeda (inside/outside), agtiisa/agteeda (near), dishiisa/diisheeda (on top), hoostiisa/hoosteeda (beneath), geestiisa/geesteeda (at the side), hortiisa/horteeda (in front), dabadiisa/dabadeeda (behind), dartiisa/darteeda (because of), dhexdooda (among). Each has masc/fem form matching the associated noun.

Negative present progressive (conjugation 1): keenayda/keenaysid/keenaya/keenaysa/keenayna/keenaysaan/keenayaan. Alternative: infinitive + maayo/maysid/mayso/mayno/maysaan/maayaan. Past progressive negative: stem+ayn or stem+aynin (conj 1), infinitive+ayn/in (conj 2-3).
Five prefixing verbs: yiil (to be in a place, inanimate), yimi (to come), yidhi (to say), yiqiin (to know), yahay (to be). Person markers are prefixes: y- (he), t- (you/she), n- (we), zero (I).

waxa focus construction: waxa + verbal pronoun + verb + focused noun phrase. Same meaning as baa/ayaa focus but used when NP is long (e.g., incorporates relative clause). Word order differs: WAXA (+verbal pronoun) VERB FOCUSED NP. When subject focused: subject in absolutive, reduced paradigm verb, waxa lacks subject pronoun.

Subordinate clauses: (1) all essentially noun phrases; (2) no mood classifiers or focus markers; negative word is aan instead of ma; (3) special verb forms; (4) all subordinate clauses are essentially relative clauses. Three groups: in-clauses, relative clauses, and adverbial clauses.

in-clauses (complement clauses): in + subject verbal pronoun + object + verb. Used for English 'that' clauses, 'in order to', and 'have to/must'. Subordinate verb forms: present/present progressive same as main clause negative forms (-aa->-o, -aan->-aan). Past: same as main clause with different stress-tone.

Preposition-pronoun clusters: fixed order PRONOUN + u + ku + ka + la. Single stress-tone on final vowel. Examples: ii (me+for), igu (me+in), iga (me+from), ila (me+with), kuu (you+for), kugu (you+in), kaa (from+you), kula (you+with). Preposition-preposition clusters also exist: ug, uga, ula, kaga, kula, kala.

Restrictive relative clauses use oo; appositive (non-restrictive) use ee. oo is not a relative pronoun. Appositive RCs cannot be used with undefined head nouns. Restrictive RCs may not be used with names. oo marks the clause type only.

RC verb forms depend on two factors: (1) whether head noun is subject of RC, and (2) whether head noun+RC is subject of main sentence. Four possibilities total. When HN not subject of RC + RC not subject: present=main clause negative forms, past=stress on final vowel. When HN not subject + RC is subject: same as main clause forms. When HN is subject + RC not subject: reduced paradigm absolutive. When HN is subject + RC is subject: reduced paradigm subject.

Question words: goorma (when), sidee (how), yaa (who, subject, uses reduced paradigm), kuma/tuma (who, object), maxay (what), maxaad...u (why/for what), xaggee/halkee/mee (where), -kee/-tee (which), immisa/meeqaa/intee (how many/how much). Answers must focus the requested information.

Independent pronouns: aniga (I), adiga (you sg.), isaga (he/it m.), iyada (she/it f.), innaga (we incl.), annaga (we excl.), idinka (you pl.), iyaga (they). Can stand alone, used for emphasis and focusing. Shortened forms (an, ad, is) used when suffixes added. Used in 'while' construction: pronoun + oo + appositive RC.

yahay (to be): General past has no person prefix; markers as suffixes (aha, ahayd, ahayn, ahaydeen, ahaayeen). General present uses person prefixes; stem changes from ah to i in 2nd/3rd plural (ahay, tahay, yahay, tahay, nahay, tihiin, yihiin). Reduced paradigm present: ah (absolutive), ihi (subject). No progressive form (stative verb).

yahay in subordinate clauses: same forms as main clause except reduced paradigm past tense (subject form without stress-tone). With adjectives: always use contracted form (delete ah). Attributive adjectives in RCs: zero/nothing (absolutive), -i (subject form).

Common adjectives (opposites): weyn/yar (big/small), dheer/gaaban (long/short), kulul/qabow (hot/cold), dhow/fog (near/far), culus/fudud (heavy/light), wanaagsan/xun (good/bad), macaan/qadhaadh (sweet/bitter), buuran/dhuuban (fat/thin), quruxsan/fooxxin (beautiful/ugly), jirran/ladan (sick/healthy), toosan/qalloocan (straight/curved), jilicsan/adag (soft/hard), qoyan/engegan (wet/dry), dheregsan (full), harraadsan (thirsty), gaajaysan (hungry). Stress-tone on final vowel.

Comparative: ka + adjective + yahay (e.g., ka culus tahay 'is heavier than'). Superlative: ugu + adjective + yahay (e.g., ugu weynyahay 'is the largest'). Very: aad (focused with baa/ayaa) + ii + adjective. Extra emphasis: aad iyo aad.

Attributive position adjectives: hore (first, previous), dhexe (middle, between), dambe (next, last, behind), kale (other), kasta/walba (each, every), kore/sare (upper), hoose (lower), shishe (far), soke (near).

CHAPTER 1 - SOMALI SOUNDS AND SPELLING. THE SOMALI ALPHABET. LETTER a (alif), aa, b (ba'), c (ca), d (da), dh (dha'), e (e'), ee, f (fa'), g (ga'), h (ha'), i (i), ii, j (ja'), k (ka') can never be final, kh (kha'), l (la'), m (ma') can never be final, n (na'), o, oo, q (qa'), r (ra'), s (sa'), sh (sha'), t (ta') can never be final, u, uu, w (wa'), x (xa'), y (ya'), ' (hamsa) can never be word initial. NOTE: Native Somali words never use p, v, z.

### Exercise 1 VOWEL SOUNDS. af (mouth, language), far (finger; script), ama (or), aabi (offense), abaar (drought), baa (FOCUS marker), edeb (manners), fure (key), feeg (look at/out), meel (place), kii (the one [masculine]), ilig (tooth), og (knowing), boqol (hundred), soco (walk), oon (be thirsty), doon (will/future), ul (stick), guri (house), dumar (womankind), uun (just, only), buug (book), carruur (children).

### Exercise 2 LONG VERSUS SHORT VOWELS. afaf (ka) languages vs afaaf (ka) entrance; dad (ka) people vs daad (ka) flood; gaadh (-ay) reach vs gadh (ka) beard/chin; sac (a) cow vs saac (a) hour; beri (ga) day vs beer (ta) garden; jid (ka) body vs jiidh (-ay) run over; guri (ga) house vs guuri (-yey) marry.

### Exercise 5 LONG vs SHORT CONSONANTS. abaar (draught) vs abbaar (aim at); beri (day) vs berri (tomorrow); caddow (become white) vs cadho (anger); caro (anger) vs carro (dirt); carrab (tongue) vs carro (dirt); gabal (portion) vs gabbal (daylight); hore (first) vs horree (precede); waran (spear) vs warran (inform); xabad (chest) vs xabbad (bullet).

### Exercise 12 TONE PAIRS. ardey (student [n5-m-sg]) vs ardey (students [n5-f-pl]); awr (male camel [n5-m-sg]) vs awr (male camels [n5-f-pl]); dibi (ox [n5-m-sg]) vs dibi (oxen [n5-f-pl]); ey (dog [n5-m-sg]) vs ey (dogs [n5-f-pl]); gees (horn [n2-m]) vs gees (side [n0-f]); inan (boy [n2-m]) vs inan (girl [n2-f]); islaan (old man [n2-m]) vs islaan (old woman [n2-f]); Soomaali (a Somali [n5-m-sg]) vs Soomaali (Somalis [n5-f-pl]).

GRAMMATICAL NOTES. The three most important grammatical markers come up in this lesson: Ma marks POSITIVE (non-negative) QUESTIONS; Baa marks FOCUS (new or emphasized information); Waa marks positive (non-negative) DECLARATIVE STATEMENTS. Note the WORD ORDER: baa comes after the head noun, whereas waa comes before the head noun. The pronoun adigu is the SUBJECT (-u) FORM of adiga, and waan is the DECLARATIVE FORM of aniga.

PRONOUNS: SUBJECT WAA FORM. aniga → anigu → waan (I); adiga → adigu → waad (you [sg]); isaga → isagu → wuu (he); iyada → iyadu → wey (she); annaga → annagu → waannu (we [exclusive]); innaga → innagu → weynu (we [inclusive]); idinka → idinku → weydin (you [plural]); iyaga → iyagu → wey (they).

CULTURAL NOTE. Somali NAMES consist of one's own name followed by that of one's father and one's grandfather. Thus, Cabdullaahi Axmed Ciisa means Abdullahi who is the son of Ahmed and the grandson of Issa. Somalis also greet by shaking hands, but some may maintain physical contact much longer than an American would be used to.

GRAMMAR NOTE. In this chapter the masculine noun magac (name) has the POSSESSIVE PRONOUN suffixes -ay(ga) my, -aa(ga) your, -iis(a) his, and -eed(a) her attached. The suffix -u is used to mark the SUBJECT on forms like magacaygu (my name), magaciisu (his name) and magaceedu (her name).

GRAMMATICAL NOTE. Each Somali noun has the following characteristics: GENDER - MASCULINE (k-marked) or FEMININE (t-marked); NUMBER - SINGULAR or PLURAL; DECLENSION - the way a noun is changed or inflected based on what kind of PLURAL FORM it has (as well as its gender and tone in the singular); altogether there are eight noun declensions in Somali. This means that you will ultimately have to learn four forms for each noun: (1) Singular root, (2) with article, (3) Plural form, (4) with article.

Names follow NATURAL GENDER. aabbe (/ha) father [masculine], hooyo (/da) mother [feminine], nin (ka) man [masculine], wiil (ka) boy [masculine], gabadh (dha) girl [feminine]. However, Somali is a language based on GRAMMATICAL GENDER. beri (ga) day [masculine], maalin (ta) day [feminine], magaalo (/da) town [feminine], beled (ka) town [masculine], jid (ka) road [masculine], waddo (/da) road [feminine], subax (da) morning [feminine], habeen (ka) night [masculine], lacag (ta) money [feminine], shilin (ka) shilling [masculine].

Remember that there are two kinds of DEFINITE INFORMATION: new (just being introduced in a conversation) which is marked by -a; and given (known by the speakers or already discussed) which is marked by -ii. All changes described for the ARTICLES -ka and -kii in this chapter will also apply to the DEMONSTRATIVES -kan this, -kaas that, etc.

Exercise 1-2: With masculine nouns that end in a vowel, the k-ending changes to -h-, and the vowel will match that of the suffix. So, for nouns that end in -e, change the final vowel of the root to -a and change -ka to -ha: dukaanle → dukaanlaha, hilible → hiliblaha, madaxweyne → madaxweynaha, aabbe → aabbaha, bare → baraha, buste → bustaha, fure → furaha, jaalle → jaallaha. Exercise 2: Same with -kii → -hii: dukaanle → dukaanlihii, etc.

Exercise 3-4: With masculine nouns ending in -o, change the final vowel to -a and -ka to -ha: biyo → biyaha, ilmo → ilmaha, xoolo → xoolaha, fardo → fardaha, gacmo → gacmaha, hablo → hablaha. Known info: -o → -i, -ha → -hii: biyo → biyihii, ilmo → ilmihii, xoolo → xoolihii, fardo → fardihii, gacmo → gacmihii, hablo → hablihii.

Exercise 5-6: If a masculine noun ends in -g, -w, -y, or -i, the k will change to a g: buug → buugga, ilig → iligga, rag → ragga, daw → dawga, ey → eyga, oday → odayga, askari → askariga, beri → beriga, guri → guriga, karraani → karraaniga, Soomaali → Soomaaliga, taksi → taksiga.

Exercise 7-8: If a masculine noun ends in the consonant -c, -h, -q, -kh, or -x, the k is lost, leaving only the vowel -a: dhinac → dhinaca, magac → magaca, sac → saca, rah → raha, shaah → shaaha, dhabbaakh → dhabbaakha, shiikh → shiikha, daaq → daaqa, dariiq → dariiqa, suuq → suuqa, libaax → libaaxa, madax → madaxa, wax → waxa. Known: final short a may change to i: dhinac → dhinacii/dhinicii, magac → magacii/magicii, sac → sacii/sicii, madax → madaxii/madixii, wax → waxii/wixii.

Exercise 1-2: With feminine nouns ending in -o, the t-ending changes to -d, and the vowel will match: cunto → cuntada, daawo → daawada, hooyo → hooyada, magaalo → magaalada, shaqo → shaqada, sheeko → sheekada, waddo → waddada. Known info: o→a with -dii (not parallel to masculine -i): cunto → cuntadii, daawo → daawadii, hooyo → hooyadii, magaalo → magaaladii, shaqo → shaqadii, sheeko → sheekadii, waddo → waddadii.

### Exercise 3 In dialects with feminine nouns ending in -dh, the -ta suffix changes to -dha. In other dialects these words end in -r. gabadh → gabadhdha (Alt: gabarta), eedh → feedhdha (Alt: feerta), aydh → laydhdha (Alt: layrta), joodh → qoodhdha (Alt: qoorta).

### Exercise 4 If a feminine noun ends in a vowel (other than -o) or with -d, -h, -kh, -x, -w, -y, or glottal stop the t changes to d: Talaada → Talaadada, duni → dunida, mindi → mindida, Soomaali → Soomaalida, bad → badda, dawlad → dawladda, dayuurad → dayuuradda, nabad → nabadda, wasakh → wasakhda, dhex → dhexda, subax → subaxda, da' → da'da, lo' → lo'da. Also applies to FEMININE OCCUPATION forms with -ad: askariyad → askariyadda, dhabbaakhad → dhabbaakhadda, dhakhtarad → dhakhtaradda, karraaniyad → karraaniyadda, macallimad → macallimadda.

### Exercise 5 Words ending in -l: combination of -l plus suffix -t changes both sounds to sh: basal + ta → basasha, bil + ta → bisha, dabeyl + ta → dabeysha, dul + ta → dusha, dhal + ta → dhasha, hal + ta → hasha, il + ta → isha, meel + ta → meesha, ul + ta → usha, walaal + ta → walaasha. Also Declension 7 plurals: aabbayaal → aabbayaasha, barayaal → barayaasha, furayaal → furayaasha, ilmayaal → ilmayaasha.

GRAMMATICAL NOTE. Although the imperative is not common, the singular imperative is the main citation form for each verb; you need to know it to find a verb in a Somali dictionary. It is also the form upon which most other tenses are built. Verbs represent the most complicated area of Somali grammar. The IMPERATIVE is the simplest of seven systems for each Somali verb.

PATTERN: FORMING THE PLURAL IMPERATIVE. Add -a to the singular imperative forms: gal → gala, bax → baxa, bar → bara, sheeg → sheega, fur → fura, xir → xira, keen → keena, cun → cuna, jar → jara, dir → dira, tag → taga, qor → qora, qaada → qaada, dhig → dhiga, shid → shida, hay → haya, hel → hela. If a verb ends in an -i or -e, add -ya: sii → siiya, akhri → akhriya, kari → kariya, bislee → bisleeya, safee → safeeya, samee → sameeya.

PATTERN 1: PAST TENSE VERB ENDINGS. For the PAST TENSE there are basically five endings: -ay Alt: -ey (I / he VERBED), -tay Alt: -tey (you [sg] / she VERBED), -nay Alt: -ney (we VERBED), -teen (you [pl] VERBED), -een (they VERBED). These endings are built up or compounded: -t- signals second person singular and plural you and third person feminine singular she, -n signals first person plural we, while -ay (or its alternate -ey) signals the past tense except for -een in the second and third person plural.

PATTERN 2: VERBAL PRONOUNS. These seven VERBAL PRONOUN forms must be memorized: aan (I), aad (you singular), uu (he), ay Alt: -ay (she ALSO they), aannu Alt: -aan (we exclusive), aynu Alt: -eynu (we inclusive), aydin Alt: -aad (you plural). When added to the DECLARATIVE CLASSIFIER waa, only w- is left. These also fuse with the FOCUS CLASSIFIER baa and with the INTERROGATIVE ma.

PATTERN 3: PRONOUN FUSION WITH MA INTERROGATIVE. Muqdisho maan tagey? (Did I go?), maad tagtey? (Did you?), muu tagey? (Did he?), mey tagtey? (Did she?), maannu tagney? (Did we [excl]?), meynu tagney? (Did we [incl]?), meydin tagteen? (Did you [pl]?), mey tageen? (Did they?).

PATTERN 4: FUSION WITH THE BAA FOCUS MARKER. Muqdisho baan tagey. (I went.), baad tagtey. (You went.), buu tagey. (He went.), bey tagtey. (She went.), baannu tagney. (We [excl] ...), beynu tagney. (We [incl] ...), beydin tagteen. (You [plural] ...), bey tageen. (They went.).

Each Somali VERB has the following characteristics: PERSON (First, Second, Third), GENDER (only on third person singular: Masculine vs Feminine), NUMBER (Singular vs Plural), TENSE (Past, Present, Habitual), CONJUGATION (based on Imperative Singular ending: Consonant final = Conjugation 1, Vowel final = Conjugations 2-3, Irregular = Conjugations 4-5).
